COMMENTS: There are 25 stone burial boxes at the Luod Site, with 19 large ones and 6 small ones (Adnyana, 1996: 11). Currently, there are 20 identifiable stone graves, most of which have been covered with earth. The pits at this site are large, with one of the pits being very wide and long. On one of the inner walls of this large pit is a plant symbol, which the Minahasans believe represents a grain of rice. In prehistoric times, rice was often associated with fertility, and such images are also found at Watu Pinabetengan. In addition to plant symbols, there are also symbols resembling boats.

COMMENTS: The Kosenggolan site is a stone burial site approximately 50 meters above ground level. It contains 19 stone burial boxes of various sizes. Based on the similarity of the carvings and the choice of cliff location, it is likely that the human group supporting the stone burial culture in the TNBNW area shared a similar cultural background (Azis, 2011: 13). The reason for choosing the cliff burial site was that it was strong and safe from animals and theft (Azis, 2012: 21). Other findings include pottery fragments of various sizes, both decorated and plain. These pottery fragments are likely the remains of burial containers for the deceased. Ancient humans recognized two types of burial methods: direct (primary) burial and indirect (secondary) burial, both with and without containers. The containers used were ceramic jars (vessels), pottery, or wooden crates (Sugiyanto, 2009: 6).

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Hidayat, R., & Muliarsa, I. W. (2013). Bulletin Umulolo: Media informasi pelestarian cagar budaya (Vol. 1, No. 3). Balai Pelestarian Cagar Budaya Gorontalo.
COMMENTS: Right in the center of the plot of land lies a Langke Bulawa megalithic statue, a half-body statue without legs. The statue's height from the ground to the head is 174 cm. The front of the body is 63 cm wide, the front of the head is 58 cm wide, the back of the body is 65 cm wide, and the back of the head is 33 cm wide. The head and face are decorated with vertical lines. The statue's facial features are further emphasized by forming an oval shape, with a nose, two round eyes, and two ears. The body features two arms that hug the abdomen down to the base. Between the arms are two breasts on the chest. The lower part of the body features a prominent oval-shaped depiction of the genitals.

CHARAC_LVL1: Burial / Cemetery / Kubur / Makam
BIBLIOGRAPHY: Hidayat, R., & Muliarsa, I. W. (2013). Bulletin Umulolo: Media informasi pelestarian cagar budaya (Vol. 1, No. 3). Balai Pelestarian Cagar Budaya Gorontalo.
COMMENTS: The only evidence and remains of burial activity in Pamona Cave that can still be found today are a distribution of human skeletal anatomy, several wood fragments suspected to be part of burial containers (yumu), mollusk shells, and beads associated with several human skeletal parts and teeth. Most of the human skeletal remains scattered throughout the cave are incomplete, and some of the bones are extremely fragile. The parts of the human skeleton that can still be identified by examining intact anatomical features of the human skeleton are divided into two parts: 1) the axial skeleton, consisting of the skull (cranium), face, spine, and rib cage. 2) the appendicular skeleton, consisting of the shoulder blades and collarbones.

CHARAC_LVL1: Burial / Cemetery / Kubur / Makam
BIBLIOGRAPHY: Hidayat, R., & Muliarsa, I. W. (2013). Bulletin Umulolo: Media informasi pelestarian cagar budaya (Vol. 1, No. 3). Balai Pelestarian Cagar Budaya Gorontalo.
COMMENTS: Types of archaeological remains are found in the niche and cave in the form of coffins or in local language called yumu and various piles of skulls inside the coffins, most of which have decayed and scattered irregularly. Most of the skeletons remain intact, visible from the skull shape of the head and face, teeth, ribs, shoulder blades, and femur bones. The coffins found in the niche and cave have two parts: the coffin cover and the body storage container. The coffins average have a long shape with dimensions 100 cm long and 45 cm wide. Overall, the coffin dimensions from the cover to the storage container are round. Each part of both ends of the cover and body storage container has elongated carving protruding upward and downward. The carving functions as a lock for both parts of the coffin from a wooden stick or a place to tie black fiber rope.

CHARAC_LVL1: Burial / Cemetery / Kubur / Makam
BIBLIOGRAPHY: Hidayat, R., & Muliarsa, I. W. (2013). Bulletin Umulolo: Media informasi pelestarian cagar budaya (Vol. 1, No. 3). Balai Pelestarian Cagar Budaya Gorontalo.
COMMENTS: Inside the Tangkaboba niche, various archaeological distributions were found that are almost not much different in shape and size from the types of coffin distribution finds in the niche/cave Latea I and Latea II, namely in the form of burial containers from coffins (yumu) that appear to be piled on the edge side of the niche wall and pottery fragment distributions, some of which are found inside the coffins and on the ground surface. Other distributions include skulls from various parts of the human anatomy, head skulls that are all still intact, rib bones, shoulder blades, and femur bones. Skeleton storage is now placed outside the coffins that were originally stored inside the coffins then removed, and piled with other head skulls by making racks to place the head skulls found on the edge of the Tangkaboba niche cliff wall.

COMMENTS: Watu Mpogaa is a standing stone or menhir made of monolithic rock. Some experts conclude that the function of the menhir is related as a memorial stone in ancestor worship rituals and as a grave marker. However, the Pamona ethnic community considers that Watu Mpogaa has a relationship with the spread or separation of the Pamona tribe as well as a direction indicator for each region of power for the local Baree language speakers in the past. COMMENTS: Centrally located along the major maritime route of the Sunda Island Chain, between eastern and western Indonesia, the harbour and burial sites of Sembiran and Pacung on the northern coast of Bali have produced critical evidence for reassessing the timing and impact of Island Southeast Asia's early exchange contacts with India and Mainland Southeast Asia during the late prehistoric period (200 BC-AD 500). The Pacung burials, dated from the late second century BC, revise the timing of Indian contact to at least the first century BC, based on fine Indian pottery in burial layers, and provide the earliest securely dated evidence for bronze and glass in Island Southeast Asia. New glass chemical data suggest stronger links with Vietnam and support transmission of bronze objects and casting technology to Indonesia from bronze-producing centres in north-eastern Mainland Southeast Asia. Preliminary lead isotope data also point to this region, with the exception of the Sembiran unleaded ring, and indicate melting of at least some imported bronzes for local recasting in Bali. A newly excavated volcanic tuff core, used to cast a bronze axe of an indigenous form, adds evidence for a local workshop at Sembiran. Preliminary data on gold and carnelian beads suggest links to the northern Indian subcontinent via western Mainland Southeast Asia. Overall, the new analytical data from Bali begin to fill a major gap in understanding Island Southeast Asia's role in late prehistoric trans-Asiatic networks. Archaeological open site, Bali.

A single volcanic flake was also recovered from the upper overbank deposit during extraction of sediment for dating. The Wolo Sege stone artefacts are predominantly small and morphologically undifferentiated flakes struck from cobbles by direct hard-hammer percussion, but include a bifacially and centripetally worked 'radial' core, similar to those characteristic of the Mata Menge assemblage of stone artefacts. It is now clear, however, in light of the evidence from Wolo Sege, that hominins were present on Flores by 1 Myr ago. This suggests that the non-selective, mass death of S. sondaari and giant tortoise, associated with stratigraphic evidence for a major volcanic eruption at Tangi Talo, ~0.9 Myr ago, could represent a localized or regional extinction, and that the faunal turnover may have been a result of climate change, volcanic activity or some other natural process or event. On a final note, the Wolo Sege stone artefacts, which currently comprise the oldest evidence for hominins on Flores, occur to the base of the volcanic and fluvio-lacustrine deposits that infill the Soa Basin. If hominins arrived significantly earlier than 1 Myr ago, as primitive morphological traits of the late-Pleistocene endemic species Homo floresiensis may indicate, then the sedimentary formations of the Soa Basin may be too young to provide evidence for the initial arrival of hominins on Flores, which must therefore be sought in other parts of the island.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Suryatman, Fakhri, Sardi, R., & Hakim, B. (2024). Development of Stone Flake Artifact Technology in the Early Half of Holocene at Leang Batti, South Sulawesi. Berkala Arkeologi, 40(2), 195–218. https://doi.org/10.30883/jba.v40i2.585
COMMENTS: Description: Research results show that the stone flake technology at the Leang Batti Site comprises two distinct occupation phases. The first phase is the Early Holocene occupation, estimated to have lasted between 9,000 and 7,000 years ago. The technology produced was dominated by relatively large flakes, used directly as tools without modification. Some flakes were also simply retouched, possibly only to neaten the cutting edges. This technology may have derived from the ancestral knowledge of the inhabitants before the Toalean techno-complex spread throughout the region. The second phase is the Mid-Holocene, estimated to have lasted between 7,000 and 3,500 years ago. Flake artefacts began to change due to the influence of the Toalean techno-complex entering the basic conceptual framework of the artefact makers. Chert material became increasingly dominant and smaller flakes were produced in greater quantities due to the need for small tools with more complex technology. Nevertheless, the Toalean influence was not particularly strong, possibly because the inhabitants were not yet ready to accept changes in flake tool technology that were, in fact, more demanding. The inhabitants of Leang Batti maintained their older technology to survive among other communities that had already adopted the Toalean cultural techno-complex.

The human occupation record of Gua Mo'o hono shelter, Towuti-Routa region of Southeastern Sulawesi. The Archaeology of Sulawesi: Current Research on the Pleistocene to the Historic Period.
COMMENTS: Description: The Gua Mo'o Hono sequence demonstrates that humans were active in and around the rockshelter from at least 6500 cal BP, informing on early to late Holocene subsistence and technology in Southeast Sulawesi. Spits 17 to 32 reflect a period of intensive habitation with high discard rates of flaked stone artefacts during the early 7th millennium BP. Local nodules of high-quality chert were flaked to produce cores, which in turn were extensively reduced in the production of flakes. Only a small proportion of the flakes were retouched, with many of the most extensively retouched pieces being small and steep-angled. These steeply retouched pieces likely functioned as scrapers for a variety of woodworking tasks. Notably, the Maros points and microliths of the Toalean are absent from the assemblage. This non-Toalean tool technology evidently persisted until later times, although associated with lower rates of artefact discard above Spit 8, roughly coinciding with the first appearance of pottery.

COMMENTS: Description: The mortuary practices identified in the Makpan burial show parallels with burial rites in other areas of Island Southeast Asia during the early and mid-Holocene. The most common burial type in ISEA, the tightly flexed burial, is suggested to have emerged in northern Borneo approximately 10,000 BP and dispersed slowly through ISEA (Piper, 2016). Although the body positioning of the sub-adult from Makpan could not be confirmed, the removal of skeletal elements, the application of ochre to the corpse, and the inclusion of an ochre-coated cobble with the burial all indicate similarities and cultural parallels with those recorded in both Niah and Ile Cave in the early Holocene, supporting the hypothesis of shared mortuary practices and traditions encompassing ISEA.

COMMENTS: Description: The cultural heritage remains at this site consist of nine menhirs arranged in a pattern based on their size. The largest menhir is approximately 150 cm tall, the others are smaller and stacked with stones in formations resembling tombs, with the smaller menhirs serving as headstones. There are four tomb formations, each with two small menhirs, commonly called Pahoman. According to local folklore, the site is associated with King Pucuk Umun and his followers, who are said to have retreated and meditated at Pasir Peuteuy before continuing their journey to Cibeo. Some hold that Pucuk Umun and his followers are the ancestors of the present-day Baduy people, though this remains uncertain.

COMMENTS: Description: The Batu Goong site is named after several stone artefacts in the complex that resemble gamelan/kenong instruments (goong in Sundanese). The site is located in a hilly area called Kaduguling and is more commonly known locally as Batu Goong. The complex contains twelve stones grouped within a 5.3 x 5.3 m enclosure: one central menhir, ten flat-topped cylindrical stones (palinggih) arranged around it, and one small gong-shaped artefact (kenong). This formation is known as the temu gelang formation, commonly found in megalithic traditions. One additional stone artefact lies outside the enclosure but remains partially buried. The stones are protected by a BRC fence measuring 11.12 x 11.12 m and 1.2 m high. The cylindrical stones have a relatively consistent diameter of 50-52 cm, with varying heights.

COMMENTS: Description: The site features a block of andesite stone with a flat top resembling a bed, known as a dolmen. In megalithic tradition, dolmens serve as burial grounds or places of worship, the exact function at Batu Ranjang is unknown as no associated megalithic elements such as menhirs have been found. The dolmen is supported by four neatly crafted stones bearing circular pleated carvings, with a foundation beneath to prevent sinking. Its orientation is east-west, it measures approximately 258 cm long and 99 cm wide, and is made of andesite. Atop the dolmen are two stones: one round and one slightly oval (approximately 33 cm long and 20 cm wide). Two mortar stones, thought to have served as instruments of ancestral spirit worship, are located on the south and north sides of the dolmen respectively. The dolmen is similar in form to dolmens in the Sumba region used as graves.

COMMENTS: Description: The Cidaresi Scratched Stone is an andesite monolith measuring approximately 175 cm long and 102 cm wide, located in the middle of local rice fields. It bears triangular incised marks of varying sizes, each with a hole at the centre, collectively depicting a symbol interpreted by the local community as representing female genitals (kemaluan wanita), and understood as a symbol of fertility or purity. Fertility symbols were central to the rituals of farming and livestock-raising communities who believed their harvests and herds depended on the propitiation of ancestral spirits.

Located near a river and in the middle of a plantation, the site has been fenced to prevent damage by animals and humans. COMMENTS: Description: WAI-53 Mon Ake, meaning 'secret place' in the Wauyai dialect of Ma'ya, is located in the Sabama (red mangrove) area of Kabui Bay, several metres above present mean sea level. The site comprises a single red anthropomorph and a geometric motif to the top left. The anthropomorph has two protrusions from the head, one hand with three fingers raised, and another hand without visible fingers pointing downward. The two protrusions may represent bird plumes or kain (cloth in Papuan Malay), both significant exchange valuables used as headdresses in the past.

COMMENTS: Description: WAI-74 Mol II, meaning 'behind the mountain' in the Laganyan dialect of Ma'ya, is located in northern Mayalibit Bay adjacent to Arway village, on the south side of a steep karst peninsula. The site displays both red and white rock images on a single rock face. Elders at Arway recount that their ancestors lived atop the mountain before monotheist religions, during the hongi raids - Tidore fleet raids to Raja Ampat for slaves and tribute, outlawed by the Dutch in the late nineteenth century. Panel 1 (red): one anthropomorph, a right handprint, and a faded geometric design below, elders at Anday identify the figure as a Ma'ya person adorned with kain on head and waist and holding a shield and knife. The images are located only about 0.5 m above high tide, suggesting relatively recent production. Panel 2 (white): immediately to the right of the red images, depicts a human in a boat and other now-faded designs, unknown to the Arway elders.

Panel 1 (northernmost): faded paintings depicting an anthropomorph with uplifted arms, an abstract arrow shape, two anthropomorphs in a canoe, and two marine animals, painted over a brown background below are two abstract designs and a nearby faded image possibly relating to a geometric or sailboat motif. Several metres to the south and about one metre higher: a scene showing two anthropomorphs with upraised arms above and adjacent to a sailboat, painted over a brown pigment background.

White pigment was directly applied onto a naturally iron-stained rock face. The panel depicts: one anthropomorph with a cross above it two partially eroded figures, one preserving only its head and one uplifted bent left arm with five fingers (head protrusions may represent hair, a headdress, or another feature) another figure to the right preserving only two slightly bent uplifted arms with five fingers on each hand and two abstract geometric paintings resembling the letter A, associated with tall karst islands at other sites such as Mlelen Popo and Ye Mampiar.

COMMENTS: Description: WAI-4 Kakit was first recorded in 2018. According to Yeheskial Dawa, ancestors of present-day Ambel speakers used the rockshelter as a stop during hunting trips. Continued use of the site is evidenced by black pigment words in Papuan Malay written on the karst walls. During excavations in 2024, a further set of white images was documented: four crosses situated in limestone crevices approximately 2.5 m above the ground surface, each with T-shaped endpoints and four dots produced close to the axis of each cross.

COMMENTS: Description: WAI-54 Mlelen Popo, meaning 'manta ray above' and referring to a place where a cross can be seen in the Wauyai dialect of Ma'ya, is located on the eastern face of a large peninsula of Waigeo Island on the western edge of Kabui Bay. Two panels of white pigment art with trace evidence of a brown pigment background are located along approximately 10 m of rock face, close to the modern high tide level. A shell placed in a crevice near the art may be contemporary with the paintings or later. Panel 1, near sea level: crosses, triangles, marine animals (including what appears to be a crab), and anthropomorphs or lizards with slightly bent arms with three fingers. Panel 2: a sailboat image approximately 5 m above present mean sea level, accessible by climbing (unlike the red pigment sites at Lentagin, Mon Ake, and Brambaem which lack accessible handholds).

COMMENTS: Description: WAI-55 Fafag is located on the northeast side of Fafag Island, with one panel of white paintings on a brown pigment background approximately 1 m above the low tide mark, a few centimetres above the high tide mark. The panel is grouped into three clusters. Cluster 1 (left): an anthropomorph or hybrid human-animal motif with uplifted arms and an abstract motif above. Cluster 2 (middle): an anthropomorph or hybrid with raised arms and a cross above, an anthropomorph with uplifted arms, an arrow through its torso, and a cross above, a sailboat with a smaller anthropomorph and a cross below, an anthropomorph with uplifted arms next to a cross enclosed in a circle above another anthropomorph above a forked cross, a curved abstract motif above a trapezoid, a canoe, and a half-circle divided into three segments (the trapezoid and canoe may represent a sailboat, or the trapezoid may depict an island or mountain), geometric motifs (two crosses, a triangle), a face in portrait view, and an anthropomorph with faded or back-positioned arms, below these, a canoe, a small anthropomorph, and abstract motifs resembling the letters E and T. Cluster 3 (right): several small crosses and abstract motifs, an anthropomorph with raised arms, and a curved animal design. Many figures have upraised arms with three fingers and head protrusions possibly representing hair or headdresses. Interlocutor Frans Waiganyam described the scene as a fight between local Ma'ya people and incomers represented by the figure with an arrow through its torso, possibly recalling an undocumented attack on incoming sailors. The scene may date to the late eighteenth or early nineteenth century context of increased Malay, Chinese, and European trade and Malukan raiding, or may reflect an earlier conflict between Ma'ya and Beser Biak or Malukan clans.

COMMENTS: Description: Toé Cave yielded 26.3 kg (1775 fragments) of stone artefacts, dominated by chert (n=1698), mostly from the upper half of the deposit. In Square 2N1E two peaks in artefact frequency were recorded at 60-75 cmbs and 40-55 cmbs similar peaks in Squares 1N1E and 1S0E at 65-75 cmbs and 40-45 cmbs. Three bone artefacts were recovered: two bipoints (50-60 cmbs, Squares 0N0E and 1S0E) and one unfinished fragment (30-35 cmbs, Square 0N0E). Three undecorated pottery sherds were recorded between 5 and 15 cmbs, with temper (quartz and feldspar-like inclusions) similar to sherds from Kria Cave.

COMMENTS: Description: Kria Cave yielded 1528 stone artefacts (7.5 kg total), the majority made from a relatively light, brittle chert the remainder were limestone, silicified tuff, quartzite (including a pebble used as a hammerstone), and metamorphic material. Most chert artefacts were excavated below 110 cmbs in Square 0N0E, while the distribution was more constant in Square 1N1E. In addition, 92 bone artefacts were excavated, restricted to the upper 45 cm in Square 0N0E and the upper 35 cm in Square 1N1E. Three pottery sherds were recovered from the top 10 cmbs of Square 0N0E, and a fourth at a depth of 20-25 cmbs. The pottery was tempered by quartz grains and a feldspar-like mineral, believed to derive from the Arfak mountains to the north and east of the lakes and on Waigeo, Batanta, and Salawati islands to the north and west of the Bird's Head Peninsula. One sherd was decorated with incised cross lines. Human skeletal remains were excavated from the upper levels of Square 0N0E, with small quantities also recorded in Square 1N1E.

COMMENTS: Description: Karas Cave is situated approximately 45 m above sea level on a hill in the Arguni Bay area. Rock art with various paintings of figures such as anthropomorphs, fish, geometrics, circles, pyramids, grids, and unidentified paintings were found on the cave walls. The Balai Arkeologi Papua (Papua Centre of Archaeology) excavated this site in 2012 and 2013. Minimally, two different human individuals were identified in excavation box GKQ1 (F6). Two upper second incisors (left and right) were assigned to individual Krs/649, one was selected for collagen isotope analysis, while the other was selected for enamel apatite analysis. The Krs/649 specimens were excavated from a soft, sandy loam at 104 cm below the surface, associated with charcoal, fish bones, nut shells, animal bones, two fragments of human long bones, seashells (Arcidae and Veneridae), and freshwater shells (Littorinidae, Naticidae, and Terebridae). Another sample of a human phalange assigned to individual Krs/638 was selected for collagen isotope analysis. The Krs/638 specimen was unearthed from a dark grey, soft and moist sandy loam at 120 cm from the surface. The archaeological findings associated with Krs/638 consisted of nut shells, human long bones, as well as marine and freshwater molluscs (Arcidae, Veneridae, Littorinidae).

COMMENTS: At this site, two excavation boxes were opened. The first was opened on the top of the hill, to the north-east of the second box. The human remains sampled for isotopic analysis were found in the second unit and included Ymk/1-R (radius) and Ymk/2-P (phalange), which were selected for collagen stable isotope analysis. Ymk/1-R was found at 54 cm below the surface associated with molluscs and pottery fragments. The sediment associated with this depth was dark brown in colour with grain size ranging between 2 and 0.02 mm, reflecting sandy loam. Ymk/2-P was found associated with pottery fragments at 135 cm depth, in a sediment with grain size ranging from 0.02 to 0.002 mm. One radiocarbon determination is available for this site, based on charcoal that dates to 2590±120 BP (Suroto 2016, 1). The charcoal was found in the same spit as Ymk/2-P, providing an approximate age for the specimen. No radiocarbon dating has yet been obtained for the upper spits associated with Ymk/1-R, but it can be assumed that this specimen postdates 2590±120 BP.

COMMENTS: Description: Three square-metre excavation boxes were opened on the site, given the names MMK1, MMK2, and MMK3, and excavated following 10 cm spits. Fragmentary human remains were found in all three excavations. MMK1 is located 18 m south-west from MMK2, while MMK3 is located 15 m east of MMK1. Two teeth from the Mamorikotey site, including a lower premolar (MMK_333) and lower molar (MMK_419), from two different humans were selected for enamel apatite analysis in this study. The lower premolar (MMK_333) was found in MMK3 at 25 cm depth. The sediment associated with this depth was dark brown, wet, and fine in texture. The findings associated with MMK_333 include human incisors, pottery fragments, shells, marsupial teeth, seeds, the femur of a pig, molar teeth, fish bones and teeth, and several unidentified animal bones. A charcoal sample was radiocarbon dated to 2520±50 BP (IHME-3995) from MMK3 at a depth of 115 cm, providing a maximum possible age for MMK_333. The charcoal was found associated with marine shells and pig bones. The lower molar (MMK_419) was found in MMK1, at 35 cm from the surface. The sediment associated with this depth was dark brown, moist and fine in texture with a pH of 7. No radiocarbon dates have yet been obtained from the MMK1 excavation unit, but the lower molar likely postdates 2520±50 BP.

COMMENTS: Description: One square metre test pit was opened at this site, where archaeological material was recovered from 1 to 100 cm from the datum level. These remains included pottery fragments, several marsupial mandible fragments, pig molars, and shells. Two samples of human long bones, including an ulna and fibula, from two different individuals were selected for collagen stable isotope analysis. Specimen NMT/1-U (ulna) was encountered at 48 cm from the surface, while the NMT/2-F (fibula) was unearthed at 81 cm from the surface. The radiocarbon dating analysis of a charcoal sample from a depth of 76 cm presents a date of 110±40 BP (IHME-3994). This suggests that the human specimens selected for isotope analysis are very recent.

At this site, a bronze axe was accidentally encountered by Obed Wally (a local Sentanian person living in this area) during his gardening activity as he planted siapu (a root crop) on the hillside. The bronze axe (13.5 cm long, 9.5 cm wide, and 1.5 cm thick) is crescent-shaped, with the simple wedge gradually developing into a flange. The bronze axe seems to have been produced using the cire perdue wax casting technique.

The local people at Dondai believe that the Yope site was used as a settlement by their ancestors in the past. Fishermen who used to dive to catch fish found pottery fragments decorated with crocodile motifs and net weights made from burnt clay on the lake floor. Based on the research results and interpretation of the surrounding environment, the Yope site may have been used as a settlement by a community of fishing people in the past, who built stilt houses above the surface of the lake.

The stone engraving at this site was decorated with geometric designs.

COMMENTS: Description: Based on interviews with local people, this site was occupied by the people who moved from Kwadeware to the west. Exploration of the lake floor at this site successfully recovered pottery fragments, bone tools, and an arrowhead made from soang wood (Xanthostemon sp.). Several house posts made from soang wood have also been found at the Ayauge site, and local people say that this wood was used for making stilt houses in the past. Logs of these trees can last hundreds of years, so traditionally they were used as house posts by the Sentani people.

Pottery was found distributed on the cave floor together with human remains, glass beads, and other materials.

COMMENTS: Description: This site is located on a small bay in the north-west part of Ogar Island. Red paintings are found on an overhanging cliff, facing west. The remains are scattered along the cliff for approximately 25 m, 2 to 8 m above sea level (asl). They mostly decorate the lower part of the cliff| however, some more faded paintings can also be found further up. One faded Matutuo is still visible (Plate 73). Here are also remains of a yellow painting, possibly also representing a matutuo and a boomerang (Plate 74)| several red motifs are already washed away or badly faded. Some hand stencils can also be seen. This site was the first listed in Roder's catalogue. He also indicated that not far from this cliff, further west, another cliff showed remains of faded red paintings.

COMMENTS: Description: Site number 2 of Roder's catalogue is a small island, situated between the Ogar and the Arguni Islands. On the southern part of the island, on an overhanging cliff approximately 4-5 m asl, some red marks as well as yellow pigments are visible. Some hand stencils and other figures are already faded. They are scattered along the wall for about 9 m. In a small niche are remains of a red anthropomorphic figure with both hands raised and legs spread apart. Unfortunately, someone has thickened the outline of this figure with a pencil to reveal it more clearly. This painting is in Roder's book. His informant told Roder that this figure is a female matutuo, characterized by the absence of the pointed hat.

COMMENTS: Description: Pictures here are still very clear, as in Roder's illustration. There are two red objects: the lower one looks like a bullet with a triangular shape, while the other is a long tubular form with two maize com-shaped objects hanging underneath. The length of the pictures does not exceed 50 cm.

CHARAC_LVL1: Rock art site / Petroglyph / Pictograph / Hand stencil
BIBLIOGRAPHY: Arifin, K., & Delanghe, P. (2004). Rock art in West Papua. UNESCO. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000135558
COMMENTS: Description: The bay has a couple of islets and is well protected from the open sea. Paintings have been drawn about 5 m asl, most of them already faded. Of the five groups of paintings illustrated by Roder in his book, only one can be found and it is less clear than in Roder's illustration (Risatot, Figure 1), (Plate 92). The beautiful anthropomorphic figure which has a headdress like a helmet and a spiral penis or tail in Roder's book is now already faded, and part of the face has peeled off. A turtle painted on the left of the anthropomorphic figure mentioned earlier is faded, as are other figures and lines. A solid sun with rays can still be seen clearly. Remains of other yellowish-red pigments are scattered on this panel, but cannot be differentiated into figures. Roder described Risatot as a complex of paintings located in different places in this bay. Some were located in a cave. However, he did not mention the exact locality, except that this cave was situated approximately 100 m from the painted gallery and part of it was already ruined. At the entrance, Roder recorded remains of human and animal bones, ceramics, a model of a small boat, and a shell trumpet scattered on the ground. Roder got the impression that this place was used to keep not only the dead, but also important objects. He also recorded a wooden sculpture of an ancestor (matutua) in this cave complete with a charm of dugong teeth. Such a sculpture was also found on one of the islets in this bay. Roder mentioned that there were four small matutuo figures in a corner, but they were very fragile, and when he touched.
